rv.q: It’s a heartrending, unforgettable performance—perhaps Ms. O’Hara’s finest to date.
Deeper, wiser and warmer than it was in its premiere at Off Broadway’s Atlantic Theater Company last year.
Director Michael Greif’s production is shot through with heartache and hangovers, and worth all the squirming in your seat.

The musical adaptation of 'Days of Wine and Roses' is a deeply moving and expertly crafted production that showcases the destructive power of addiction while highlighting the strength of the human spirit.
If Days and Wine and Roses isn’t exactly galvanizing—it’s too classy for that—it is effectively sober.

The show is caught in the middle, but it’s still a beautifully directed, acted, written and composed piece about, yes, alcohol but also about our responsibility to the very few people in our lives who depend on us absolutely for their own happiness and survival.
Despite these headwinds, I liked it.
Inebriation isn’t ultimately all that interesting to watch, particularly when you know how much more a star can do.
The show...has a searing power that leaves you both stirred and shaken.
But this musical — a passion-lacking passion project from collaborators Adam Guettel and Craig Lucas — doesn’t go down easy.

The only major criticism to level at “Days of Wine and Roses” is that it took Guettel so long to write his third musical, which can easily take its place as one of the few great musicals of this century.
Alcoholism is a jealous lover and demands full obedience of its victims.
Foster couldn’t have found a tastier palate cleanser than Winnifred, nor a more charmed home to rest her weary, ever-so-busy head.

So it is for Joe and Kirsten Clay, and by not shying away from the good vibrations that controlled substances promise, this new Days of Wine and Roses is a small step in the right direction toward making a difference in America’s current addiction crisis.
That’s all the rationale needed to set the parameters for this bold, unflinching musical gaze at drinking to cruel excess.
O’Hara and James are capable of leaving us not simply pensive, but elated and shattered, if they had a show that would let them.
Under Michael Greif’s vigorous, compassionate direction, it proves, if not a flawless work, a superior showcase for their extraordinary gifts.
Depressing and harrowing as it is, it’s not the kind of show we often get around these parts.
The subject matter is almost corrosively downbeat but, with its two leads at the top of their game, the one-act musical becomes a cathartic, deeply felt tonic.

The two stars carry “Days of Wine and Roses,” their exquisite voices bringing out the brilliance of Adam Guettel’s jazz-inflected, often operatic score, and investing the characters’ rocky emotional journeys with a credibility that few other performers could match.
James and O'Hara's sparkling chemistry is effortless, entirely convincing us of their deep love even in their darkest moments — and those moments become all the more arresting as a result.
Days of Wine and Roses is an affecting, unblinking portrayal of the reality of dealing with addiction that’s seldom seen on Broadway.
Instead, here they play a couple on a relentlessly degrading, depressing, downward spiral.
Days of Wine and Roses on Broadway is a work of astonishing artistry, sophistication and emotional depth.
Days of Wine and Roses is the best new musical of the Broadway season.
It is a must-see that is superbly performed.
Unless you have a heart of stone, you will be moved.

Even though that thought might linger for some time after leaving the theatre, what may dampen that euphoric feeling is the realization that although that might have been two of the best performances you have ever seen, the musical itself was not up to par.
But with the need to have the characters and the strong supporting ensemble break into song at regular intervals the dark consequences of alcoholism seem in danger of trivialization.
But this is an off-putting exercise on both a narrative and a musical level — one that may leaving you pining for less wine and many more roses.
As a musical, it makes you thirsty for something with more of a sting.
Lucas adds nothing to Miller's original work that doesn't diminish it, which is an unscalable problem.
